questions.question: What three properties distinguish a VRF from an ordinary pseudorandom function?
options: Pseudorandomness, uniqueness, and provability — the output is unpredictable, fully determined by (sk, m), and accompanied by a verifiable proof
Secrecy, integrity, and non-repudiation — the same properties as a digital signature scheme
Collision resistance, preimage resistance, and second-preimage resistance — the same as a cryptographic hash function
Unforgeability, aggregability, and threshold-shareability — the same properties as BLS signatures
questions.explanation: VRF = pseudorandomness (output indistinguishable from random before proof is revealed) + uniqueness (exactly one valid output per (sk, m)) + provability (proof lets anyone verify the output is correct).

questions.question: Why can't a blockchain use an ordinary hash H(seed) for leader election randomness?
options: A malicious proposer can grind seeds until H(seed) produces a favorable output, biasing the election
Hash functions are too slow to evaluate once per slot at network-wide scale
Hash outputs are not uniform over the integers, making leader selection unfair
Hash functions are deterministic, so the leader schedule would repeat every epoch
questions.explanation: An adversary who controls the seed input can enumerate many seeds and choose one that benefits them. A VRF output is pseudorandom only before the proof is revealed and cannot be selectively disclosed.

questions.question: In the DH-VRF construction, what is gamma = H^sk mod p?
options: The core VRF output: pseudorandom because it requires sk to compute, and unique because there is exactly one value for a given (sk, m)
The Schnorr nonce commitment used to derive the Fiat-Shamir challenge
The public key corresponding to the message hash, used only during proof verification
A hash of the secret key and message used to avoid leaking sk in the proof
questions.explanation: gamma = H^sk is the VRF's fundamental output. It requires sk to compute (pseudorandomness) and is uniquely determined by sk and m (uniqueness). beta = SHA-256(gamma) is the final byte output.

questions.question: What does the dleq proof (c, s) in this VRF certify?
options: That the same secret key sk was used to compute both pk = g^sk and gamma = H^sk, without revealing sk
That the message m was hashed correctly to produce H before gamma was computed
That the nonce k used during evaluation is uniformly random and was not reused
That gamma lies in the correct subgroup of order q and is not a degenerate element
questions.explanation: The dleq proof is a Schnorr-style zero-knowledge proof of discrete-log equality: log_g(pk) == log_H(gamma) == sk. It lets a verifier confirm the output is correct without learning sk.

questions.question: Why does vrf_proof_to_hash return SHA-256(gamma) instead of gamma directly?
options: To produce a fixed-length uniform byte string and remove any algebraic structure from the group element that could leak information
To make the output longer so it can be split into multiple random values
Because gamma must remain secret; hashing it makes beta public without exposing gamma
To satisfy the Fiat-Shamir requirement that all outputs are in the same hash domain
questions.explanation: Group elements have algebraic structure (quadratic residuosity, subgroup membership) that could distinguish them from uniform random bytes. Hashing via SHA-256 maps to a fixed 32-byte uniform output with no observable structure.

questions.question: What happens if the nonce k is reused across two VRF evaluations with the same sk?
options: The two (c, s) pairs yield a linear system that exposes sk, identical to Schnorr nonce reuse
Verification fails for both proofs because the Fiat-Shamir challenge detects duplicate nonces
The two gamma values become identical, revealing that the same message was signed twice
Only the second proof is insecure; the first evaluation remains safe
questions.explanation: With k reused: s1 = k - sk*c1 and s2 = k - sk*c2. Subtracting gives sk = (s1 - s2) / (c2 - c1) mod q. RFC 9381 mandates deterministic nonce derivation from (sk, m, randomness) to prevent this.

questions.question: In hash_to_group for a safe prime p = 2q+1, why does squaring (candidate^2 mod p) produce an element of the q-order subgroup?
options: For a safe prime, the squares form the unique subgroup of order q = (p-1)/2; every quadratic residue has order dividing q
Squaring doubles the exponent, which halves the order of any element in Z_p*
The generator g=2 is itself a square, so any power of g is also a square
Squaring applies the Legendre symbol which maps all elements into {0, 1} mod p
questions.explanation: Z_p* has order p-1 = 2q. The subgroup of quadratic residues (squares) has order (p-1)/2 = q. Squaring a uniformly random non-trivial element lands in this unique q-order subgroup.

questions.question: Which check must a VRF verifier perform to prevent a malicious prover from submitting a gamma outside the correct subgroup?
options: Verify that pow(gamma, q, p) == 1, confirming gamma has order dividing q
Verify that gamma < p/2, confirming it is in the lower half of the field
Verify that gamma is not equal to pk, confirming distinct group elements were used
Verify that SHA-256(gamma) has a certain prefix, confirming the hash-to-group was applied
questions.explanation: A valid group element of order q satisfies g^q = 1 (mod p). Checking pow(gamma, q, p) == 1 rejects elements outside the subgroup. Skipping this check may allow crafted gamma values to bypass the proof.
